newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank's Gaddum urges banks to divest holdings.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank's Gaddum urges banks to divest holdings.

text.p: Bundesbank Deputy President Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said on Wednesday Germany's stockmarket had yet to achieve the breakthrough it needed to attain world standards and urged banks to help by offloading some shareholdings.
He also called on the government to remove tax barriers preventing firms from becoming shareholding companies.

"Despite historic price highs on the stock exchange and successful share launches by various companies the mood appears to be depressed because all measures taken so far do not appear to have given the German stock market the big breakthrough," Gaddum said according to the text of a speech.

Banks have been accused of wielding too much power through their large stakes in industrial companies, but coming stock market legislation is widely expected to avoid rigorous measures like slapping a limit on banks' shareholdings.
Gaddum said that even though lawmakers, market organisers and major players had done much to prepare the share market for global competition, it still lacked breadth and depth.
The market could become more attractive if there were more joint stock companies and if existing share stakes were more widely distributed, he said.

"It would be desirable if banks took suitable companies public more often than they have done in the past...," Gaddum said. "This would partly deflate the recurring debate about banking power and would also contribute to strengthening and reviving the German stock market."
The speech was due to be delivered at a stock market conference in Bonn.

"Not only are there not enough listed shareholding companies," Gaddum said. "In addition, the capital of many companies is in the firm hands of family shareholders, banks, insurers and other companies.
"This part of capital is fundamentally unavailable for stock market trade."

The resulting lack of shares explained why trade concentrated on relatively few liquid stocks and why the share prices of small and medium-sized businesses were often subject to large price swings, Gaddum said.

But he had praise for the German system of universal banks, saying the tradition of close ties between banks and industrial companies had proved an important stabilising factor in Germany's corporate scene.
In addition, banks sometimes had good reason for buying and holding on to industrial share stakes.
But such ties could also conserve existing structures and the resulting ease of obtaining credit tended to prevent companies from floating their shares on the stock market, Gaddum said.

He also called on the government to remove differences in taxation which put partnerships and single-person companies at an advantage over incorporated firms and thereby hamper the formation of joint stock companies.
